To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HCV treatment uptake among HCV/HCV coinfected patients increased after introduction of DAA therapies, and the average payers’ expenditures and patients’ copayment for HCV treatment increased significantly.

HCV/HIV-coinfected patients were less likely to be initiated on HCV treatment in the pre-DAAA period compared to HCV-monoinfected patients, but no significant difference was observed during the DAAA period.

HCV treatment initiation increased from the pre-DAAs to the post-DAAs period, especially among HVC/HIV coinfed patients, but the cost of HCV treatment per patient increased by 55%, which was driven by the high cost of DAAs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of DAA therapies on treatment initiation rates, as well as the associated costs.
the cost burden of HCV therapies for payers and HCV/HCV coinfected patients.
the early treatment uptake and the costs associated with the treatment of HCV/HIV-coinfected patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cost burden for HCV treatment increased significantly for both payers and patients.

despite the increased uptake of HCV treatment among HCV/HCV coinfected patients and a significant increase in treatment costs, the high efficacy, safety and tolerability of DAAs have resulted in improved clinical outcomes and a substantial reduction in HCV-related morbidity and mortality.
HCV/HIV coinfection was a risk factor for lower HCV treatment initiation during the pre-DAAA era but not during the post-DAAA era.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HCV/HIV-coinfected patients are more likely to initiate HCV treatments after the introduction of all-oral DAAS.
the introduction of all-oral DAAS for HCV treatment was associated with increased treatment initiation rates, but at the expense of increased costs for both payers and patients.
the HCV/HIV population is still being under-treated and the high costs of HCV treatment are a major barrier for patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cost of HCV treatment is high for both payers and patients and may limit the access of patients to these new therapies.
despite the availability of more effective, safe, and well-tolerated HCV treatments, the high drug costs associated with these therapies remain a major barrier to access for patients.
the cost burden associated with HCV treatments is substantial and may be a barrier to treatment initiation, particularly among patients with low socioeconomic status.
